newsitem.title: USA: PacifiCorp to acquire Britain's Energy Group.
newsitem.headline: PacifiCorp to acquire Britain's Energy Group.

text.p: PacifiCorp Friday agreed to buy Britain's Energy Group Plc for $9.6 billion in a deal that would create one of the world's biggest energy companies just as the British market prepares for deregulation in 1998.

PacifiCorp, which operates in seven states and Australia, said it will pay about 6.96 pounds ($11.35) a share for Energy Group. It will also assume $3.8 billion of debt held by Britain's biggest electricity distributor.
"This will make us the first vertically integrated utility on three different continents," said Dick O'Brien, chief financial officer of the Portland, Oregon-based company.
The merged company will have 5 million electric and gas customers, 17,000 megawatts of generation capacity and more than 10 billion tons of coal reserves.
As part of the deal, PacifiCorp will sell its Pacific Telecom unit for $1.5 billion to Century Telephone Enterprises Inc., which will also assume $700 million in debt.
That revenue, along with the planned sale of two smaller units, will allow PacifiCorp to carry out the transaction without issuing a large block of new stock.
The companies said they did not expect the merger to result in significant job cuts, since few operations overlap.
PacifiCorp officials said the merger is expected to boost earnings in the first year after the deal is completed, which is expected in late summer or early fall.

Energy Group, which owns Britain's electric utility, Eastern Electricity, and U.S.-Australian coal producer Peabody, has been considered a takeover target since it was spun off from the conglomerate Hanson Plc in February.
PacifiCorp hopes to leverage the British utility's experience with deregulation into the U.S. market, which is being moved away from regulated monopoly utilities.
Britain's electricity market will be fully open to competition by April while California will become the first U.S. state to allow retail competition starting in January.
PacifiCorp also expects benefits from Energy Group's Peabody coal, the world's largest private coal producer, and from its U.S. power marketing subsidiary, Citizens Power.
"We plan to continue to build off our fuel resources and generation, leading on value all the way through to the light switch," O'Brien said.
The deal has been approved by the boards of directors of both companies, and is subject to regulatory approval in Britain and the United States.
PacifiCorp wants to avoid Federal Energy Regulatory Commission oversight of the deal, which involves combining the companies's FERC-licensed power marketing units.
"They are breaking a little bit of new ground here, but a FERC review would just take too long," said Ed Tirello, an analyst at NatWest Securities.

PacifiCorp's O'Brien said the combined power marketing operations would be conducted under one license. "We are not going to take control of Citizens' agreements and assets. That would put us under FERC jurisdiction," he noted.

Regulatory concerns kept Energy Group's shares below the bid price, though the company reported a 30 percent rise in income to 317 million pounds ($517 million) for the six months ended March 31, analysts said. Energy Group stock fell 2 pence (3 cents) to 645 pence ($10.52) on the London Stock Exchange.
"There's much more uncertainty over this deal, with a new and untried Labour government and the possibility of a windfall tax," said one London analyst who asked not to be identified.

The new Labour government, which won a landslide victory on May 1, has criticised the previous government's takeover policy under which all but one of Britain's 12 regional electricity companies were swallowed up by buyers.
Privatised utilities also face a one-time tax on excess profits, which the government has vowed to include in its first budget on July 2.
Uncertainty over the tax has kept utility stocks under pressure. But analysts said there were scant competitive or regulatory grounds for the new government to block a takeover.

"I can't see any obvious problems for the government," the analyst said. He said since Eastern Electricity has already been privatised, the latest deal is a "change of ownership rather than structure."
Some analysts believe Tony Blair's government might seek customer compensation such as price cuts to approve the bid.
